title: Amaranth vs. Quinoa: Nutrition Compared

seo.title: Amaranth vs. Quinoa: Nutrition Compared
seo.meta_description: Cooked quinoa and amaranth have similar protein; quinoa usually has a little more fiber, while amaranth stands out for calcium and a creamier texture.
seo.search_intent: Compare amaranth and quinoa for protein, fiber, minerals, calories, and cooking.

excerpt: Per 100 g cooked, quinoa is around 120 calories and 4.4 g protein; amaranth about 102 calories and 3.8 g. Quinoa usually has slightly more fiber, while amaranth contributes notable calcium and iron and cooks to a much creamier texture.
content_html:
Quinoa and amaranth often sit in the same “ancient grain” aisle because both are cooked like grains without being grasses, but they behave quite differently in a bowl. Per 100 g cooked, quinoa is about 120 calories, 4.4 g protein, and 2.8 g fiber; cooked amaranth is roughly 102 calories, 3.8 g protein, and about 2 g fiber. The macro differences are modest. Texture and some minerals separate them more clearly.

Cooked nutrition side by side

QuinoaAmaranth
Calories~120~102
Protein~4.4 g~3.8 g
Fiber~2.8 g~2 g
TextureSeparate, fluffy seedsCreamier, more cohesive

Quinoa has only about 18 more calories and 0.6 g more protein per 100 g. In a 180 g cooked portion, that works out to roughly 216 calories and 7.9 g protein from quinoa versus 184 calories and 6.8 g from amaranth. That is not a large enough protein gap to drive the whole decision.

Amaranth's mineral profile is a more useful distinction

Amaranth is notable for calcium, iron, and magnesium. Quinoa also contributes iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, so neither wins every micronutrient. Values also shift dramatically between dry and cooked foods because both grains absorb water.

That water effect matters. Comparing dry amaranth with cooked quinoa would make amaranth look far more nutrient-dense almost across the board, but the comparison would not represent equivalent portions.

Good protein quality does not mean high protein quantity

Both quinoa and amaranth contain all essential amino acids and have a relatively favorable lysine profile compared with many cereal grains. That describes protein quality. It does not turn either one into a concentrated protein food.

A cooked serving generally contributes only around 7–8 g protein. If protein is a major goal for the meal, pair either pseudocereal with lentils, beans, soy foods, eggs, dairy, or another main protein source.

Texture may matter more than the nutrition panel

Quinoa keeps a more separate, rice-like texture and works well in salads, bowls, and side dishes. Amaranth releases more starch and becomes creamy, making it useful for porridge, compact fillings, or recipes that benefit from binding.

Which one should you choose?

Choose quinoa when you want a fluffy grain-like base and amaranth when you want a creamier texture or a different mineral mix. The nutritional differences are too small for a universal winner; they are complementary foods rather than better and worse versions of the same thing.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Quinoa has a small cooked-weight edge, about 4.4 g/100 g versus roughly 3.8 g/100 g for amaranth.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Quinoa usually provides slightly more, around 2.8 g/100 g cooked.
